Editor's note: CNN has asked its journalists across the country to offer their thoughts on how the economic crisis is affecting their cities. In this installment, Bob Crowley reports from Boston, Massachusetts. Hardware store owner Brendan Kenney says "people who have money should go out and spend it." BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) -- Brendan Kenney has seen enough bad news about the economy. "I'm also getting tired of being worried," he says. His family has been running a small hardware store in Brookline, Massachusetts, just outside Boston, for about 56 years. He says business has slowed down a little, but mostly because winter is normally the slow time of year for them. Though he hopes the stimulus plan will help his and other small businesses, he believes people shouldn't be afraid. "I think the American consumer holds a lot of power," he continues. "I think people who have money should go out and spend it." Like many in the Boston area, Kenney doesn't want to hear more discouraging stories and sees that as part of the problem. "It's just negative story after negative story, kind of creating a crisis of confidence."  Watch Boston-area reaction to the economic slump » . South of Boston, Jose Nieto, from Plainville, has his own reasons to be discouraged. Between September and October of last year, he was laid off twice. Nieto, a civil engineer who works on road construction projects, had felt fortunate. After losing his job of 14 years, he was able to find employment after only being out of work for two weeks. After being on the new job for three weeks, however, he got called into the boss's office. "I said, 'Oh, no. My God, not again.'" He was faced with looking for work in an industry that traditionally slows down in the winter months. "It's more than losing your job. It gives you a feeling of rejection," he says. Yet, Nieto feels this is a time to learn valuable lessons, especially for those who need to dip into their savings when unemployment checks don't cover all of the bills. "I think a lot of people will learn from this situation, and, going forward, they'll try to save more money." He has been trying to stay healthy, busy and positive. Passing the time working on projects in his basement workshop and taking yoga classes has helped him get through the rough spots, and his luck is turning. He was offered a job that starts in March. "It is a relief, because I'm employed," he says, "however, I'm taking a job for much less money." Nieto believes that most employers cannot afford to hire at the salaries they could offer in the past. Like Kenney's hardware store, Sue Stein's American craft gallery, also in Brookline, is not seeing any major shifts in her business, yet. "Our business has been certainly down, but not devastating," she says. Fire Opal, her gallery, sells everything from earrings to pottery to scarves, all made by artists from around the country. To keep her business healthy, she says, she is trying to make adjustments like buying less merchandise. But she is changing her approach to her customers as well. She says she tries to keep "understanding that people are having a hard time and trying to find things that are more in their price range." Like Kenney and Nieto, Stein is also trying to stay optimistic. "I think if we all are very careful," she says, "we'll sort of ride it out and then things will adjust."

“I think a lot of people will learn from this situation, and, going forward, they’ll try to save more money.”

“It is a relief, because I’m employed,” he says. “However, I’m taking a job for much less money.”

Like Kenney and Nieto, Stein is also trying to remain optimistic.

“I think if we all are very careful,” she says, “we’ll sort of ride it out and then things will adjust.”

**Editor’s note:** CNN invited reporters around the United States to share observations about how the economic downturn is being felt in their communities. In this report, Bob Crowley writes from Boston, Massachusetts.

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) — Brendan Kenney, who owns a hardware store, believes that “people who have money should go out and spend it.”

Kenney says he has had enough of the steady stream of grim economic news. “I’m also getting tired of being worried,” he says.

For roughly 56 years, his family has operated a small hardware shop in Brookline, Massachusetts, just outside Boston. According to Kenney, sales have dipped somewhat, although he notes that winter is typically the slowest season for the store.

While he hopes the federal stimulus package will benefit his business and other small companies, Kenney says consumers should not let fear take over.

“I think the American consumer holds a lot of power,” he says. “I think people who have money should go out and spend it.”

Kenney, like many others in the Boston region, says he is weary of hearing one gloomy report after another and believes that the constant negativity is contributing to the problem.

“It’s just negative story after negative story, kind of creating a crisis of confidence.”

South of Boston, Plainville resident Jose Nieto has faced his own setbacks. Between September and October of last year, he lost two jobs.

Nieto, a civil engineer involved in road construction projects, initially considered himself lucky. After being laid off from a position he had held for 14 years, he found another job after only two weeks of unemployment.

But after just three weeks in the new role, he was summoned to his boss’s office.

“I said, ‘Oh, no. My God, not again,’” he recalls.

He then had to search for work in a field that typically becomes slower during the winter season.

“It’s more than losing your job. It gives you a feeling of rejection,” Nieto says.

Even so, Nieto says the experience can teach important lessons, particularly to people who must rely on savings when unemployment benefits are not enough to cover every bill.

“I think a lot of people will learn from this situation, and, going forward, they’ll try to save more money.”

To get through the difficult period, he has focused on staying active, healthy and upbeat. Spending time on projects in his basement workshop and attending yoga classes have helped him manage the stress. His situation is now improving: he has been offered a job that begins in March.

“It is a relief, because I’m employed,” he says, “however, I’m taking a job for much less money.”

Nieto says he thinks many employers simply cannot pay the kinds of salaries they once could.

Back in Brookline, another small business owner, Sue Stein, says her American craft gallery has not yet experienced drastic changes. Like Kenney’s hardware store, her shop has seen some decline, but nothing catastrophic.

“Our business has been certainly down, but not devastating,” she says.

Stein’s gallery, Fire Opal, sells handmade items created by artists from across the country, including earrings, pottery and scarves.

To protect the business, Stein says she is making changes, such as purchasing less inventory. She is also adjusting the way she works with shoppers.

She says she tries to remain mindful that customers are struggling financially and to help them find items that better fit their budgets.

Like Kenney and Nieto, Stein is working to maintain a hopeful outlook.

“I think if we all are very careful,” she says, “we’ll sort of ride it out and then things will adjust.”

However, he believes the bigger problem is not only the decline in sales, but also the fear created by constant negative economic news. In his view, widespread anxiety is damaging consumer confidence and causing people to pull back more than necessary.

Kenney argues that consumers who still have money should continue spending, at least within reasonable limits. He believes they have significant power to help support the economy. By continuing to shop, hire services, and make purchases they can afford, consumers can help keep local businesses open and prevent the downturn from becoming worse.

For others, the economic crisis has been far more personal. Jose Nieto, a civil engineer from Plainville, experienced the hardship directly when he was laid off twice within two months. The situation was especially difficult because he had previously held a job for 14 years before losing it.

Nieto says unemployment is painful not only because of the financial pressure it creates, but also because of the emotional toll. Losing a job can feel like a form of rejection, leaving people discouraged and questioning their value. For many workers, the loss of employment affects their identity as much as their income.

Despite his discouragement, Nieto believes the crisis can also teach important lessons. He says it has shown many people the importance of savings, especially when unemployment benefits are not enough to cover basic needs. For those forced to rely on their own resources, the experience may be difficult, but it can also serve as a reminder to prepare more carefully for uncertain times.

CNN’s report on the economic crisis in the Boston area looks beyond national statistics and Wall Street headlines to show how the downturn is affecting people in everyday life. Through local voices, the story presents a picture of an economy shaped not only by job losses and reduced spending, but also by fear, uncertainty, and a loss of confidence among consumers.

One perspective comes from a local hardware store owner, who explains that the health of his business depends heavily on whether customers feel secure enough to spend money. In better times, people might come in for home improvement projects, repairs, tools, or supplies without much hesitation. But during an economic crisis, even necessary purchases can be delayed. The store owner worries that when people hear constant negative news about layoffs, falling markets, and financial instability, they become more cautious. That caution can quickly affect small businesses, which rely on steady local spending to survive.

The report also highlights the experience of a civil engineer who has been laid off twice, showing how the crisis has reached workers in professional fields as well as those in retail, service, or manufacturing jobs. His story reflects the insecurity many people feel when even stable careers no longer seem guaranteed. Being laid off once is difficult enough, but facing repeated job loss can change a person’s outlook on work, money, and the future. It can force families to rethink expenses, postpone plans, and prepare for more uncertainty.

A major theme of the report is the powerful role of psychology in the economy. Fear can become self-reinforcing: when people are worried, they spend less; when they spend less, businesses earn less; when businesses earn less, they may cut jobs or reduce hours; and those cuts create even more anxiety. In this way, negative expectations can deepen the effects of an economic downturn. The report suggests that consumer confidence is not just an abstract economic measure—it has real consequences for local shops, workers, families, and communities.

At the same time, the story points to resilience. People in the Boston area are trying to adapt by cutting unnecessary costs, searching for new work, supporting local businesses when possible, and learning to be more careful with their finances. For many, the crisis has become a lesson in preparedness: saving more, taking on less debt, planning for emergencies, and recognizing that economic stability can change quickly.

Overall, CNN’s examination of the Boston area shows that an economic crisis is not experienced only through numbers such as unemployment rates or stock prices. It is felt in quieter, more personal ways: in a store owner’s concern about whether customers will keep coming through the door, in a laid-off engineer’s struggle to regain stability, and in the everyday decisions families make about what they can and cannot afford. The report emphasizes that recovery depends not only on government action or financial markets, but also on restoring confidence, encouraging responsible spending, and helping people regain a sense of security about the future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style local news article from Boston about how the economic crisis is affecting residents and small businesses, including quotes from a hardware store owner, a laid-off civil engineer, and an art gallery owner.
counterfactuals.output:
**BOSTON —** As prices remain stubbornly high and hiring slows across key industries, many Boston residents and small business owners say the economic strain is becoming harder to absorb — showing up in everything from delayed home repairs to empty gallery openings and a growing sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

In neighborhoods from Dorchester to Jamaica Plain, residents say the cost of groceries, rent, utilities and transportation has forced them to rethink everyday decisions. For small businesses, the pressure is two-sided: customers are spending less, while owners face higher costs for inventory, wages, insurance and rent.

At **Harbor & Sons Hardware**, a family-run store in South Boston, owner **Mark Donnelly** said customers are still coming in — but they’re buying differently.

“People used to come in and say, ‘I’m redoing the bathroom,’ or ‘I’m building a deck,’” Donnelly said. “Now it’s, ‘What’s the cheapest way to patch this?’ or ‘Can I make this last another six months?’ You can tell folks are trying to stretch every dollar.”

Donnelly said the cost of basic supplies has risen significantly over the past few years, and he has had to make difficult decisions about what to stock.

“If I raise prices too much, I lose customers,” he said. “If I don’t raise them, I can’t cover my own bills. That’s the tightrope every small business is walking right now.”

For some Boston residents, the crisis is personal and immediate.

**Elena Morales**, a civil engineer from Roslindale, said she was laid off this spring after her firm lost several commercial development contracts. She has applied for dozens of jobs, but says the market feels far different than it did just a few years ago.

“I did everything I was supposed to do — got the degree, built experience, worked hard,” Morales said. “But when projects get delayed or canceled, people like me are suddenly out of work. It’s scary because Boston is not an easy city to be unemployed in.”

Morales said she has cut back on dining out, canceled subscriptions and postponed medical appointments to manage expenses while looking for work.

“The rent doesn’t pause just because your paycheck does,” she said. “You start making choices you never thought you’d have to make.”

The economic uncertainty is also hitting Boston’s arts community, where galleries, performance venues and independent artists rely heavily on discretionary spending.

In the South End, **Nina Patel**, owner of **Citrine Gallery**, said foot traffic has declined and buyers are more hesitant.

“People still love art. They still come in, they still look, they still talk about pieces,” Patel said. “But fewer people are buying. A painting that might have sold in a week now sits for months.”

Patel said rising rent and event costs have made it harder to keep the gallery open. She has started hosting lower-cost community events and offering payment plans for buyers, but says the broader mood is cautious.

“Art is often one of the first things people cut when money gets tight,” she said. “But for artists, this isn’t a luxury — it’s their livelihood.”

Economists have warned that even when broader indicators show signs of stability, many households continue to feel squeezed because wages have not kept pace with costs in high-expense cities like Boston. Housing remains one of the biggest burdens, with renters and small businesses alike facing steep monthly payments.

City officials have pointed to small business grants, workforce programs and housing initiatives as part of the response, but residents and business owners say relief can feel slow compared with the speed of their bills.

Back at Harbor & Sons Hardware, Donnelly said he remains hopeful but cautious.

“Boston people are tough,” he said. “They support each other. But toughness doesn’t pay the electric bill. We need things to ease up before more small businesses disappear.”

For Morales, the goal is simpler: finding steady work and regaining a sense of control.

“I love this city,” she said. “I just want to be able to afford to stay here.”

# In Boston, Recession Pressures Hit Housing, Hiring and Household Budgets

**BOSTON, Massachusetts —** As part of a nationwide look at how the recession is affecting American cities, Boston presents a complicated picture: a city with world-class hospitals, universities and technology firms, but also one where high housing costs and rising everyday expenses are magnifying the pain for working families.

Across the city, residents say the slowdown is being felt most sharply in rent, groceries, transportation and job security. While Boston’s economy is more insulated than many due to its concentration of health care, higher education and biotech, those strengths have not shielded everyone from cutbacks and uncertainty.

For many households, the biggest strain remains housing. Boston was already one of the most expensive rental markets in the country before the downturn, and residents with modest or fixed incomes are finding fewer ways to absorb added costs. Some renters say they are doubling up with relatives or delaying moves because they cannot afford security deposits, broker fees or higher monthly payments.

Small businesses are also feeling the squeeze. Restaurant owners and shopkeepers in neighborhoods such as Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Roxbury and East Boston report that customers are spending more cautiously. Some have reduced hours, delayed hiring or cut back on inventory as foot traffic becomes less predictable.

The labor market remains uneven. Workers in hospitals, universities and some technology sectors may have more stability, but service workers, gig workers, retail employees and recent graduates are facing tougher conditions. Hiring has slowed in some industries, and workers who lose jobs say it can take longer to find comparable pay.

City officials and nonprofit groups say demand for assistance has increased. Food pantries, rental-support programs and community organizations are seeing more residents who are employed but still unable to cover basic costs. Advocates warn that even a mild recession can be severe in a city where the cost of living was already beyond reach for many families.

At the same time, Boston’s economic foundation gives it advantages. The region’s hospitals, research institutions and universities continue to attract investment and talent. Major employers in medicine, education and life sciences help stabilize the local economy, even as other sectors weaken.

Still, for residents living paycheck to paycheck, the broader indicators matter less than the monthly math. In Boston, the recession is not only a story of job losses or business closures — it is a story of an already expensive city becoming harder to afford.

**Consumer confidence rises, but layoffs keep recovery hopes in check**  
*Boston, Massachusetts — 2009*

As the recession grinds through its second year, Americans are showing tentative signs of optimism — even as layoffs, tight credit and weak sales continue to weigh heavily on households and small businesses.

Recent readings on consumer confidence suggest that some people believe the worst of the economic downturn may be easing. Gas prices are lower than last summer’s peaks, the stock market has recovered some ground from its lows, and federal stimulus money is beginning to move through the economy.

But on Main Street, the mood remains cautious.

In Boston, small-business owners say customers are still watching every dollar. Restaurants are trimming hours, retailers are offering deeper discounts, and service companies are delaying hiring until demand becomes more predictable.

“We’re seeing people come back, but they’re not spending the way they used to,” said one local shop owner. “They’ll buy what they need, but they think twice before adding anything extra.”

That hesitation is one reason economists warn that improving confidence does not necessarily mean a quick recovery. Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of the U.S. economy, and without steady job growth, many families are unlikely to return to pre-recession habits.

Layoffs remain the biggest obstacle. Companies across industries — from manufacturing and finance to media and technology — have continued to cut payrolls in an effort to reduce costs. Even workers who still have jobs say they are saving more and spending less out of fear they could be next.

Small businesses are feeling the pressure from both sides. Many rely on consumer spending to stay afloat, but they also depend on credit to manage payroll, inventory and expansion. Since the financial crisis, loans have become harder to obtain, particularly for newer firms or those with declining revenue.

Business advocates say that leaves many owners stuck: too uncertain to hire, too stretched to invest, and too dependent on customers who are themselves worried about job security.

Still, there are signs of resilience. Some entrepreneurs are using the downturn to renegotiate leases, find discounted equipment or shift into lower-cost online sales. Others say the recession has forced them to operate more efficiently.

Economists say that kind of adaptation could help position small firms for growth once demand returns.

For now, optimism is measured rather than exuberant. Analysts say confidence can improve before the labor market does, but a sustained recovery will require fewer layoffs, stronger credit conditions and a return of consumer spending.

In neighborhoods around Boston, that recovery still feels uneven. Coffee shops are busy, but customers linger over smaller orders. Contractors report more inquiries, but fewer signed deals. Help-wanted signs are rare.

The result is an economy caught between fear and hope.

Many consumers believe the slump will end. Far fewer are ready to spend as if it already has.

## Economic Strain Deepens Across Greater Boston as Small Businesses and Families Feel the Squeeze

**BOSTON —** Across Greater Boston, the signs of economic stress are showing up in familiar places: at neighborhood hardware stores, in suburban family budgets, and inside small galleries that rely on discretionary spending. Rising rents, higher borrowing costs, stubborn inflation, and uneven consumer demand have created a difficult climate for residents and small businesses alike.

For **Brendan Kenney**, who works at a hardware store in Brookline, the shift has been hard to miss.

“People still come in for the essentials,” Kenney said. “If a pipe breaks or a lock needs replacing, they’re here. But the bigger projects — renovations, upgrades, things people used to do when they felt more comfortable — those have slowed down.”

Kenney said customers are comparing prices more carefully, buying only what they need, and putting off household improvements that once helped drive steady sales.

“You can tell people are thinking twice,” he said. “A few years ago, someone might come in and say, ‘I’m redoing the whole bathroom.’ Now it’s more like, ‘What’s the cheapest way to patch this for now?’”

### Families Cut Back as Costs Rise

The pressure extends well beyond Boston’s urban core. In Plainville, **Jose Nieto** said his household has had to make difficult adjustments as prices for groceries, insurance, utilities, and transportation remain high.

“It feels like every month there’s something else going up,” Nieto said. “You make a budget, and then the bill comes in higher than expected. You try to save, but it gets eaten up.”

Nieto said his family has cut back on dining out, delayed car repairs when possible, and become more cautious about travel and entertainment.

“We’re not in crisis every day,” he said. “But there’s no breathing room. That’s the part that wears on you.”

Economists say that sentiment is becoming increasingly common in high-cost regions like eastern Massachusetts, where wages have risen for many workers but often not enough to offset housing costs and inflation in essential goods and services.

### Small Businesses Face a Delicate Balancing Act

In Brookline and Boston, small-business owners say they are caught between rising operating costs and customers who are more price-sensitive than ever. Commercial rents, insurance premiums, inventory costs, and credit card fees have all climbed, leaving owners with few easy options.

Passing those costs on to customers can risk losing sales. Absorbing them can mean thinner margins or reduced staffing.

At **Fire Opal gallery**, **Sue Stein** said the slowdown has been especially visible in purchases that depend on consumer confidence.

“Art and jewelry are meaningful purchases, but they’re also purchases people can postpone,” Stein said. “When people feel uncertain, they still come in, they still look, they still appreciate the work — but they may wait.”

Stein said galleries and independent retailers depend heavily on foot traffic, loyal customers, and a sense of economic optimism.

“Small businesses aren’t just numbers on a spreadsheet,” she said. “They’re part of the character of a neighborhood. But it takes a lot to keep the doors open right now.”

### A Regional Economy Under Pressure

Greater Boston remains one of the country’s most dynamic regional economies, anchored by universities, hospitals, biotechnology, finance, and technology. But that strength has not insulated residents from the pressures of affordability.

Housing remains one of the largest burdens. Renters face some of the highest monthly costs in the country, while prospective homebuyers are squeezed by elevated prices and mortgage rates. For many, even a stable job no longer guarantees financial security.

The result is an economy that can appear strong on paper while feeling fragile at the household level.

“You hear that the economy is doing fine,” Nieto said. “Maybe it is for some people. But for a lot of us, it doesn’t feel that way.”

### Waiting for Relief

For now, many residents and business owners say they are simply trying to hold on — cutting costs, delaying plans, and hoping for stability.

Kenney said the mood among customers is not hopeless, but it is cautious.

“People are resilient,” he said. “They figure things out. But you can feel the stress. Everyone’s trying to make their money go further.”

Stein said she hopes customers continue to support local businesses even in small ways.

“You don’t have to make a big purchase to help,” she said. “Walking in, sharing our work, buying something modest — it all matters.”

As the Boston area heads into the coming months, the region’s economic story may depend less on headline numbers and more on whether ordinary households and independent businesses can regain a sense of stability.

For many, that recovery still feels just out of reach.
